metadata.description:
Case name: New Jersey v. New York

Opinion filed: 1998-05-26

Docket No.: 120

Citations:
• 140 L. Ed. 2d 993
• 118 S. Ct. 1726
• 523 U.S. 767
• 1998 U.S. LEXIS 3405

Case holding summaries:
• charging Georgia with the knowledge that South Carolina was cultivating the territory in question
• stating that it is well established "`that open and notorious adverse possession is evidence of notice; not of the adverse holding only, but of the title under which the possession is held' "
• finding prescription where United States Army Corps of Engineers had performed some work on territory in dispute
• rejecting argument that prescription is not possible where the United States holds title to land
• noting that "Louisiana has always asserted [ownership of the disputed area]; and that Mississippi has repeatedly recognized it, and not until recently has disputed it"
• noting that the United States does not have the power to reestablish boundary lines
• noting that people living in the disputed territory gave allegiance to West Virginia
• noting that both States had adopted the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey line by statute and used it for nearly 80 years
• noting that litigation of disputes between States "is obviously a poor alternative to negotiation between the interested States"
• rejecting Michigan's claim of "excusable ignorance" on the ground that "[t]he material facts . . . have been so obvious that knowledge of them on the part of the Michigan authorities, if it were not shown, as it is shown, by the evidence, must necessarily be assumed"
• "It seems appropriate to repeat the suggestion . . . that the parties endeavor with consent of Congress to adjust their boundaries"
• noting that all but a handful of the residents of the disputed territory considered themselves citizens of Tennessee
• there was evidence that both States were familiar with congressional resolutions locating the disputed territory in Vermont but New Hampshire did not object
• "[T]he practical construction of the boundary by the acts of the two states and of their inhabitants tends to support our interpretation of the Order-in-Council of 1764"
• "`[T]o ascertain [the] meaning [of treaties] we may look beyond the written words to . . . the practical construction adopted by the parties' "
• civil suit for assault committed `upon government property at Ellis Island'
• "[C]ourts have no power to substitute their own notions of an `equitable apportionment' for the apportionment chosen by Congress"
• referring to "the rule of property law that artificial fill belongs to the owner of the submerged land onto which it is deposited" (citing Marine Railway & Coal Co. v. United States, 257 U. S. 47, 65 (1921))
• declining to redraw the boundary between New Jersey and New York for reasons of practicality and convenience
• explaining the littoral boundaries remained as they were before artificial land-filling increased the surface area of Ellis Island
• resolving territorial dispute between New York and New Jersey regarding Ellis Island by following "common-law rule [that] speaks in the silence of the Compact"
• noting that a prescriptive period of 64 years is "not insufficient as a matter of general law"
• describing the "natural and ordinary meaning of `jurisdiction'"
• describing the "natural and ordinary meaning of `jurisdiction'"
• stating that courts “must pass over” arguments of amici that the named party to the case “has in effect renounced”
• looking to historical censuses and maps to determine which parts of Ellis Island lay in New York and New Jersey
• stating that courts “must pass over” arguments of amici that the named party to the case “has in effect renounced”
• “[T]he silence of the Compact was on the subject of settled law governing avulsion, which the parties’ silence showed no intent to modify”
